title: Application Architecture Styles (Archetypes)
overview: Choose architecture styles from quality attributes, data needs and team capacity. Compare frontend options, monoliths, microservices, hexagonal design, serverless, and Lambda/Kappa data processing. The modern archetypes add decisions about blast radius, placement, ownership, offline work and repeatable operations; combine them only where their benefits justify the cost.
big_ideas: Every style is a trade-off: monoliths are simple and fast but hard to scale per component; distributed styles buy scalability and fault isolation at the cost of operational complexity.
Choose an architecture from drivers: domain, architecture characteristics, data, organisation and teams, and sync vs async communication.
Hexagonal architecture keeps the domain at the centre, reached only through ports and adapters, so it can be driven by users, tests or scripts and run on any infrastructure.
Lambda = batch + speed + serving layers (accurate but two pipelines); Kappa = one stream pipeline + serving (simpler, lower latency, harder reprocessing).
Event-driven is a principle applied across monoliths, microservices, serverless and data architectures for loose coupling and responsiveness.
AKF scale cube: x = replication (clones), y = functional decomposition (services/functions), z = data partitioning (sharding).
PWAs favour web reach and shared code; native integration can offer deeper platform capabilities. Verify offline, push and hardware needs on target devices.
Modern archetypes compose with classic ones; each answers a different question and has a stated 'do not use when'.

sections.title: Industry context and full stack layers
sections.summary: Where software engineering is heading and what a full stack cloud native application is made of, with its overwhelming choice of technologies.

notes.h: Cloud native app: the whole stack
notes.lead: A cloud native application is a whole stack, and the platform is part of the design.
items: **User experience** and **client**
**API server**
**Data/event store**
**Container or function platform**
**GitOps delivery**
notes.foot: How code is **packaged and deployed** shapes scalability and delivery speed as much as the code does.

notes.h: Five investment areas for engineering leaders
items: **APIs and integration**
**Automation** (pipelines)
**Experience and design**
**Platforms and tools**
**Quality/testing/security** → a 'digital immune system'

notes.lead: The lecture presents forecasts about AI-assisted engineering.
items: **2028/2030 scenarios** → specification-driven workflows
**Smaller AI-augmented teams**
**Predictions, not settled facts**: clear constraints, review and verification still matter

notes.lead: The problem the rest of the deck solves.
items: **Every layer** has many languages, frameworks and protocols
**Architects need a disciplined way** to choose a style from requirements rather than from fashion

terms.def: Everything from the user interface down through API server, data store and the platform it runs on.
Containers-as-a-Service / Functions-as-a-Service: compute platforms that run the back end.
Practices and technologies for quality, testing and security that keep digital products resilient.

check.q: A team's code is well structured, but releases take two weeks because deployments are manual and the app runs on hand-built VMs. A teammate says 'architecture is about the code, the platform is ops' business'. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No**: in a **cloud native full stack**, the **platform is part of the design**.
items: **Packaging** as containers or functions + delivery through **Git-driven pipelines** → shape **scalability** and **delivery speed** as much as the code does
Here the **platform is the bottleneck**
**Fix**: **automated pipelines** + a **container or function platform** → cuts the two-week cycle more than **refactoring code** would

check.q: A manager reads that AI-assisted engineering will soon make teams smaller and work 'specification-driven', and proposes cutting architecture reviews because 'the AI writes the code'. How do you respond?

items: **Forecasts, not settled facts**: that is how the lecture presents them
Even if they come true → **specifications and architectural constraints** become the main input to **AI-generated code**
So clear **quality attributes**, **review** and **verification** matter **more, not less**
a.foot: Cutting reviews removes the **check** on whether the generated code **meets the constraints**.

sections.title: Progressive Web Apps vs native apps
sections.summary: Front-end delivery options: PWAs (broad reach, one codebase) versus native and cross-platform native apps (more capability), plus WebAssembly.

items: **PWA** → web distribution; can add installation, offline caching, push and background work where the browser supports them
**Native or cross-platform native** → platform integration and app-store distribution, with extra platform-specific work

items.t: **Choose a PWA** for speed to market, low cost, broad reach, SEO, instant server-side updates
**Choose cross-platform native (React Native, Flutter)** for feature-rich apps needing near-native performance, deep hardware access (camera, sensors) and app store presence

items: **Vary by device/browser**: installation, notifications, background work, hardware APIs
**Offline operation requires** deliberate caching, local data and synchronisation
**A PWA label** does not make every feature work offline
**Portable instruction format** executed by a **sandboxed runtime** in browsers or other hosts
**Supports** compute-heavy modules and edge runtimes
**The host** determines which capabilities it can access

terms.def: Progressive Web App: a website that behaves like an installable app (offline, push, home-screen icon).
Browser background script that caches content so a PWA works offline.
Portable binary instruction format executed by compatible sandboxed runtimes in browsers, servers or edge environments.
Shared application code targeting multiple native platforms, with framework-specific runtime and platform integrations.

check.q: A retailer wants a mobile shopping experience launched within 2 months, on a small budget, and found through search engines. PWA or native?

items: **One web codebase** + **instant server-side updates**
**Broad reach** + **search discoverability**
→ fits the **deadline and budget**
**Check**: the features it needs (**push notifications**, **offline cart viewing**) work on the **target browsers**
a.foot: **Native** only justified if a required capability **couldn't be delivered on the web**.

check.q: Field inspectors must work for hours without signal, capture photos and read a Bluetooth sensor, and the app must be in the app stores. Native (or cross-platform native) or a PWA, and what does the choice mean for the backend?

sub: **API versioning**, because installed app versions **update slowly**

check.q: A team says 'we built a PWA, so it works offline'. What would you check?

items: **Which screens and data are cached**
**How local writes are stored**
**How they sync** and **resolve conflicts** when the connection returns
a.foot: A PWA **can cache and work offline where the browser supports it**, but the label doesn't make **every feature offline-capable**.

check.q: A web app needs to run a compute-heavy image filter in the browser, and the JavaScript version is too slow. What option does the lecture suggest, and what limits it?

items: **Portable instruction format** run by a **sandboxed runtime**
Suits **compute-heavy modules** in **browsers** or at the **edge**
**Limit**: its **host** decides what **capabilities** it can access
a.foot: → speeds up **computation**, but doesn't give the **hardware access** a native app has.

visuals.title: PWA vs native vs cross-platform native
rows: Installed via app store; icon on home screen
Offline/push features require implementation and platform support

sections.title: Choosing an architecture and architectural thinking
sections.summary: How an architect decides: factors to weigh, the shift from hand-off to collaboration, the four dimensions of architecture, characteristics and Attribute Driven Design.

notes.lead: Pick an architecture from drivers, not preference:
items: **The domain**
**Architecture characteristics** that affect structure
**Data architecture**
**Organisational factors** and **team/ops knowledge**
**Domain-architecture isomorphism** → the system's shape matches the problem's shape
**Communication** → whether services communicate synchronously or asynchronously
**Characteristics** → the qualities to achieve, e.g. scalability, availability, testability
**Decisions** → long-term choices such as database type, number of services, how they communicate; they guide dev teams
**Style** → overall shape, like a building plan
**Logical components** → functional blocks such as inventory or payment
**Traditional** → architect fixed characteristics, style and components and threw them over a wall to developers
**Modern** → continuous collaboration; architect leads and mentors; feedback flows from code back into the architecture

notes.lead: The method that ties it together.

terms.def: The quality attributes (the '-ilities') the system must achieve.
The overall shape of the system, e.g. layered, microservices, event-driven.
Method that turns drivers, especially quality attributes, into structures using tactics and patterns.
How well the architecture's structure matches the shape of the problem domain.

check.q: In a design review, someone lists 'use a replicated NoSQL store' under the system's characteristics. What is wrong with that, and how would you rewrite it?

items: **Characteristics** = qualities to achieve, e.g. **availability above 99.9%**, **tolerance of a zone failure**
**Decisions** = **long-term choices** made to achieve them, e.g. the **replicated store**
**Rewrite**: write the **characteristic first**, then record the decision with the **characteristic it serves**
a.foot: → the decision can be **revisited if the requirement changes**.

check.q: An architect delivered a full design document 6 months ago, and the developers have since quietly worked around half of it. What went wrong, and what model would fix it?

items: **What went wrong**: the design was **thrown over the wall** → went **stale** as **implementation realities** appeared
**Fix**: the architect **leads and mentors within the team**
**Feedback from code** changes the architecture
a.foot: **Cost**: the architect's **ongoing time**; but the design **stays true to the code**.

check.q: A team must design a new system using Attribute Driven Design but starts by choosing a microservices pattern. What step have they skipped, and what should ADD produce?

items: **Skipped: the drivers** → **purpose**, **primary functionality**, **quality attributes**, **constraints**, **concerns**
**Design concepts** (**patterns**, **tactics**, **reference architectures**) are chosen to **satisfy those drivers**

sections.title: Monolithic vs distributed; microservices
sections.summary: The core split between monolithic and distributed styles, a taxonomy of styles, and the pros and cons of monolith vs microservices using an e-commerce example.

items: **Monolith** → deploys as one application; may have well-separated modules
**Microservices** → deploy independently; own data through service boundaries
**Distributed systems** → broader than microservices; need not follow one database-per-service model

sub: any fault can crash the whole process

items: **Anti-pattern** → big ball of mud
notes.foot: Distribution can improve **independent capacity and isolation** but adds **latency, partial failures and coordination**.
Rule of thumb: **small teams and simple apps → (modular) monolith**; **large, complex, fast-scaling apps → microservices**.

terms.def: A monolith with no discernible structure (an anti-pattern).
Core system plus plug-in modules; listed as the IoT-style monolithic pattern.
Distributed style using replicated in-memory data grids to avoid database bottlenecks.
A monolith organised into well-separated modules inside one deployable.

check.q: A startup with 4 developers is building an MVP whose features will change weekly. Monolith or microservices?

items: **One thing** to build, deploy and debug
**No network hops**
Team **can't absorb** microservices' **operational overhead**
Keep **modules well separated** → a part that later needs **independent scaling** can be **extracted**
a.foot: **Revisit** when the **team or load grows**.

check.q: After moving to microservices, a crash in the recommendation service still makes the whole product page time out. Why didn't fault isolation help, and what would?

items: **Why isolation didn't help**: separate processes **contain the crash**, but the product page calls the recommendation service **synchronously and waits** → the failure **spreads through the call**
**Fix**: **timeouts**, a **circuit breaker** and **graceful degradation**, e.g. showing the page **without recommendations**
a.foot: **Isolation** is a property you have to **design for**; it doesn't come from **deployment alone**.

check.q: A team splitting a monolith asks what it gives up by moving to microservices. Give the two biggest costs for an e-commerce shop where Cart calls Catalog.

sub: Cart's call to Catalog now adds **network latency**
e.g. keeping **prices in carts** aligned with the **catalogue**

items: Also **operational overhead** grows: more **deployments**, **monitoring** and **tracing**
a.foot: These costs are justified when **independent scaling**, **releases** and **fault isolation** are needed.

visuals.title: Monolith vs microservices
rows: Single codebase, developed as one unit
Separate services, each with its own codebase and database
One application to deploy and version
Replicate the whole application on multiple servers
An issue in any module can bring down the whole process
Codebase gets harder to change as it grows
Harder to monitor and manage: operational overhead, network latency, data consistency

sections.title: Hexagonal and serverless architectures
sections.summary: Two styles that move boundaries: hexagonal (ports and adapters around a pure domain) and serverless (event-triggered functions on provider-managed infrastructure).

items: **Layers separated**: Application, Domain, Infrastructure
**Dependencies point inward** to the Domain
**Outside world** (users, other systems, databases, tests, CI/CD) connects through **adapters on ports**
**Payoff** → driven equally by users, programs, tests or batch scripts; tested in isolation from real devices and databases
**Event-triggered cloud functions** (e.g. AWS Lambda) run on demand
**Provider scales resources in real time**, within configured and platform capacity limits

sub: building serverless structures can be labour-intensive

items: **Hexagonal** → shielding the domain from infrastructure through interfaces
**Serverless** → outsourcing infrastructure
**Combine well** → e.g. a function whose core logic is a hexagon with adapters for triggers and stores
**Serverless suits** sporadic, event-driven load, **not** steady latency-critical work

terms.def: Ports are interfaces the domain defines; adapters plug real technologies (UI, DB, queues, tests) into them.
Extra latency when a serverless function is invoked with no warm instance ready.

check.q: A team's order logic can only be tested against a real database and a running message broker, so tests take 20 minutes. How would hexagonal architecture change this?

items: **Domain core**: the order logic depends **only on ports** (interfaces)
**Adapters** for the **database** and **broker** on the outside
**Tests** drive the domain through a **test adapter**; database and broker replaced with **fakes**
→ **business logic tested in seconds**
a.foot: Keep a **smaller set of integration tests** for the **real adapters**.

check.q: A payments API has steady traffic around the clock and a strict 50 ms latency target. A teammate proposes serverless functions. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No**: long-running **containers or VMs** suit **steady, latency-critical** load.
items: **Cold starts** → threaten the **latency target**
**Constant usage** → the **pay-per-use saving** disappears
You also accept **less control** and **lock-in**
a.foot: **Serverless** would fit **sporadic, event-driven** parts, such as **sending receipts**.

check.q: A team builds a function-based service and later wants to move part of it off that provider. How could combining hexagonal design with serverless have helped?

items: Function's **business logic** sits in a **hexagonal core**
**Trigger** and **data stores** = **adapters**
→ to **move providers** or run in a **container**, **only the adapters** need rewriting
**Serverless outsources infrastructure**; **hexagonal shields the domain** from it
a.foot: Together they **reduce the lock-in cost** of serverless.

center.label: Application core
center.detail: Application, Domain and Infrastructure are explicitly separated; dependencies point toward the Domain.

items.label: Users and partners
items.detail: Reach the core through ports and the API gateway; the app can equally be driven by programs, automated tests or batch scripts.

items.label: Data stores
items.detail: External and internal data stores sit behind adapters.

items.label: Test, CI/CD extensions
items.detail: Lets the core be developed and tested in isolation from its run-time devices and databases.

items.label: Infrastructure adapters
items.detail: Platform and run time, infrastructure, tools and frameworks stay outside the core.

sections.title: Lambda, Kappa, IoT, event-driven, multi-cluster, AI
sections.summary: Data-centric and cross-cutting archetypes: the two big-data processing styles, IoT layering, event-driven design, multi-cluster deployments, AI archetypes, and how all archetypes relate.

sub: batch layer: historical data, recomputing results such as ML models

items: **Lambda pro** → accurate, batch layer as source of truth; **con** → two pipelines to maintain
**Kappa** → one stream engine for real-time and reprocessing, plus a serving layer
**Kappa pro** → simpler, low latency; **con** → stateful processing and complex reprocessing are harder

notes.h: Event-driven: a principle, not just a style
items: **Built around events** → significant state changes
**Loose coupling**
**Independent horizontal scaling** of consumers
**Real-time responsiveness**
**Can be applied on top of any other architecture**
**IoT** → smart things → networks/gateways → middleware (storage, analytics) → applications
**Multi-cluster/hybrid cloud** → spreads workloads across Kubernetes clusters for resilience, geo-distribution or compliance

sub: predictive AI: classification, clustering, regression, detection

items: **Monoliths** → small simple apps
**Microservices** → large complex apps
**Serverless** → event-driven or sporadic loads
**Lambda/Kappa** → data-centric work
**They combine** → microservices can be built from serverless functions; data pipelines often run on serverless functions

terms.def: Batch + speed + serving layers combining accurate history and fast real-time results.
Single stream-processing pipeline plus serving layer; reprocess by replaying the stream.
Components communicate by producing and reacting to events rather than direct calls.
Predictive analyses and forecasts from existing data; generative produces new content.
Running workloads across several Kubernetes clusters, across clouds and on-premises.

check.q: A ride-hailing company needs surge prices updated within seconds and also retrains its pricing model on 3 years of trip history every night. Lambda or Kappa?

items: **Speed layer**: streams **trip events** → **near-real-time surge prices**
**Batch layer**: **recomputes the model** over **full history**
**Serving layer**: exposes both
a.foot: **Cost**: maintaining **two pipelines that must agree**. **Kappa** would be simpler if retraining could be done by **replaying the stream**, but reprocessing **years of history** through **one stream engine** is harder.

check.q: A monolith needs to notify inventory, email and analytics when an order is placed, and each new consumer currently means editing the order code. Must the team move to microservices to fix this?

a.lead: **No**: **event-driven** is a principle that can be applied **on top of any style**.
items: Monolith publishes an **'order placed' event**; consumers **subscribe**
→ **loose coupling**
→ consumers **scale independently**
→ **new consumers** added **without editing order code**
a.foot: **Cost**: **eventual consistency** + the need to **monitor event flows**.

check.q: A company runs one Kubernetes cluster in one region and must now serve EU customers whose data must stay in the EU. Which archetype helps, and what does it cost?

items: **EU cluster** keeps **EU workloads and data in the EU**
Puts **compute closer** to those users
**Limits the impact** of **one cluster failing**
a.foot: **Cost**: operating **several clusters consistently**, **routing users** to the right cluster, and the **reporting and data work** across them.

visuals.title: Lambda vs Kappa
rows: Batch layer re-computes historical data; speed layer gives low-latency results
Single stream processing engine handles real-time data and continuous reprocessing
Handles real-time and historical data; batch layer is the source of truth
Two separate pipelines to maintain; operational overhead
State management; hard to handle complex transformations or reprocessing

sections.title: Modern composables, scale cube and evolution
sections.summary: Why classic styles are not enough, the AKF scale cube, and the historical path from monoliths to packaged business capabilities.

notes.lead: Classic styles only answer 'how do I decompose logic?' Modern archetypes answer other questions:
items: **Cell-based** → blast radius
**Edge-native** → where compute runs
**Micro-frontends** → UI decomposition
**Multi-runtime/sidecar** → where distributed capabilities live
**Data mesh/lakehouse** → data ownership
**Local-first** → offline
**MACH/PBC** → business composition
**Platform engineering** → repeatable operation
notes.foot: They **compose with, not replace**, the classic styles.

items: **x = replication** → clones behind a load balancer, replicated databases
**y = functional decomposition** → split into services or functions
**z = data partitioning** → shard by key, data per service
notes.foot: **Diagnose the bottleneck**, then pick the axis.

notes.lead: Architecture evolved toward composable business capabilities:
items: **Monolith**
**2-tier**
**3-tier** (UX/logic/data)
**SOA**
**Web-scale services**
**Software-defined microservices** with outer and inner APIs, plus IoT
**Packaged services** with edge computing
notes.foot: **3-tier splits by technical layer**; **microservices split by business capability**.

terms.def: Three ways to scale: clone (x), split by function (y), split by data (z).
Partitioning data across databases by a key (z-axis scaling).
Service-Oriented Architecture: coarse-grained shared services exposed via service APIs.

check.q: After adding app servers, the database becomes the bottleneck. Which scale-cube axis would you use next?

items: **Reads** → **replicas** or **caching** (**x axis** on the data tier)
**Writes** on **independent records** → **shard** by a suitable key (**z axis**)
**Heavy workload** → split it into its own **service and store** (**y axis**) → **isolates** it
a.foot: None of these fixes a **poorly designed slow query**, so **check that first**.

check.q: A team describes its 3-tier app (web, logic, database) as 'already microservices because it has separate tiers'. What is the structural difference?

items: **3-tier**: split by **technical layer** → one business change still **touches every tier**; tiers **deploy together**
**Microservices**: split **vertically by business capability**; each service **owns its logic and data** and **deploys independently**
a.foot: The 3-tier app can **scale tiers separately** but **not capabilities**.

check.q: A SaaS's checkout path is overloaded during sales, but the search and account features are not. Which scale-cube axis fits, and why not just add more clones?

a.lead: **y axis** (**functional decomposition**): split **checkout** into its own service.
items: → checkout **scales on its own**
**Cloning the whole app (x axis)** also scales **search and accounts** that don't need it → **wastes capacity**
Cloning **doesn't isolate checkout failures**
a.foot: **Cost**: a new **service boundary** and its **data ownership**.

visuals.title: AKF scale cube (The Art of Scalability)

items.label: X axis
items.detail: E.g. load balancing several copies, MySQL master-slave cluster, NoSQL replication.

items.label: Y axis
items.detail: E.g. split business logic into functions, serverless functions, hybrid cloud solutions.

items.label: Z axis
items.detail: E.g. parameter-based sharding, store data in micro service, spread data over several databases.

sections.title: Appendix: cells, edge, micro-frontends, sidecars, data mesh
sections.summary: What, why, when and trade-offs for the first five modern composable archetypes.

items: **Router** assigns users or tenants to independent **full-stack cells**
**No cross-cell runtime calls**; **cell-by-cell releases**
**Failure** affects the assigned group: roughly **1/N** only for equally sized cells

sub: automation needed to operate many environments

notes.lead: Pushes compute and some state near users.
items: **Runtime** → V8 isolates or Wasm, millisecond cold starts
**State** → eventually consistent edge storage; origin as system of record
**Use for** tight latency or residency (auth, personalisation, A/B routing)
**Avoid for** heavy compute or strong consistency
**Expect** limited runtimes, hard debugging, lock-in

notes.lead: Extend team independence to the UI.
items: **Teams own vertical slices** (UI, API, data), composed at build, edge or run time
**Backend-for-Frontend** → each experience (web, mobile, kiosk) gets its own
**Use when** many teams share one UI, or replacing a legacy front end incrementally
**Not for** a single front-end team → duplicated payloads, design consistency and shared state costs

notes.lead: Moves cross-cutting capability out of libraries.
items: **Sidecar** (service mesh, Dapr) provides discovery, mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, telemetry **uniformly across languages**
**Effect** → resilience and security become platform decisions
**Costs** → an extra hop, memory, a control plane
**Rarely justified** below about a **dozen services in one language**

notes.lead: Data mesh is the data-plane counterpart of microservices.
items: **Central team** → becomes a platform provider
**Needs governance maturity first**
**Lakehouse** → open table formats giving ACID, schema evolution, time travel on object storage; **bronze/silver/gold medallion** refinement
**Lakehouse** can be data mesh's technical base; **not the same as Lambda's layers**

terms.def: How much of the system or user base a single failure affects.
A dedicated backend per client experience that aggregates and tailors downstream services.
Helper container beside a service handling cross-cutting concerns like mTLS and retries.
Decentralised data ownership where domains publish governed data products.
Progressive refinement layers from raw to cleaned to business-ready data in a lakehouse.

check.q: A bad deploy to a multi-tenant SaaS took down all 4,000 customers at once. Which archetype limits this, and what does it cost?

items: **Router** assigns **tenants** to **independent full-stack cells**
**No cross-cell calls**
Releases roll out **cell by cell** → a bad deploy hits **one cell first**
**10 equal cells** → roughly **400 customers** affected
a.foot: **Costs**: **duplicated capacity**, a **router that becomes critical**, harder **cross-cell reporting**, and the **automation to run many environments**.

check.q: A team of five Java services proposes adding a sidecar service mesh for retries and telemetry. Would you approve it?

items: A mesh adds an **extra network hop**, **memory per pod** and a **control plane**
Lecture: **rarely justified below about a dozen services** in **one language**
There a **shared library** can give the same **retries and telemetry**
a.foot: A requirement for **uniform mTLS**, or a move to **several languages**, would change the answer.

check.q: One front-end team builds a single web app and is considering micro-frontends to 'be modern'. What would you advise?

items: **Micro-frontends** extend **team independence** to the **UI**
Pay off when **many teams share one UI** or a **legacy front end** is being replaced **piece by piece**
With **one team** → **duplicated payloads**, **design-consistency** work and **shared-state** problems, with **no independence gained**
a.foot: A **separate backend for each experience (BFF)** may still help if web and mobile need **different APIs**.

check.q: A company bought a lakehouse and declared it has 'a data mesh'. What is missing?

items: **Lakehouse** = a **storage and processing base**: **open table formats** with **ACID**, **schema evolution** and **time travel** on **object storage**

sub: **Domain teams own their data as products** with **contracts and quality**

a.foot: Without them, it is still a **central data platform**.

check.q: A product team wants to run personalisation and A/B routing at the edge, and also move order checkout there for speed. Which part fits edge-native, and which doesn't?

items: **Fits edge: personalisation and A/B routing** → **light**, **latency-sensitive**, can tolerate **eventually consistent edge storage**
**Keep at origin: checkout** → needs **strong consistency** with the origin **system of record**
a.foot: Edge also brings **limited runtimes**, **harder debugging** and **lock-in** → keep **edge logic small**.

sections.title: Appendix: local-first, MACH, platform engineering, selection
sections.summary: The last three modern archetypes and a guide matching each archetype to its driving concern and anti-use-case.

items: **Completes** suitable reads and writes on a **local replica**, then synchronises
**CRDTs or operational transformation** → merge supported concurrent edits
**Suits** collaboration and unreliable networks
**Limit** → merging cannot by itself protect **global invariants** (e.g. one seat sold once)
**Can complement a PWA**, rather than replace all PWA designs
**Packaged Business Capability (PBC)** → bundles the data and services of one capability (cart, pricing, tax), assembled from vendors and in-house parts
**Integration becomes the architecture** → needs a **capability map with owners**, or it becomes distributed procurement
**Internal developer platform (IDP)** run as a product
**Features** → golden paths, self-service, templates, GitOps on Kubernetes
**Measured by** adoption and **DORA metrics**
**Use when** cognitive load limits delivery
**Failure mode** → the platform team becoming a gatekeeper
**Blast radius** → cells (not small user bases)
**Latency/residency** → edge (not heavy compute or strong consistency)
**Many teams on one UI** → micro-frontends/BFF (not one team)
**Uniform capability across polyglot services** → sidecar (not few services)
**Data ownership at scale** → data mesh (not before governance)
**Offline/collaboration** → local-first (not global invariants)
**Many vendors** → MACH/PBC (not one stable channel)
**Operability** → platform/IDP (not small orgs)

terms.def: Conflict-free Replicated Data Type: data structure that merges concurrent edits automatically.
Microservices, API-first, Cloud-native SaaS, Headless.
Self-contained, assemblable unit of one business capability's data and services.
Self-service platform with golden paths so teams build and run services consistently.

check.q: A concert-ticketing app wants to be local-first so fans can pick seats offline. Where does local-first work here and where doesn't it?

items: **Works for drafts**: building a **seat selection** or a **wishlist** on the **local replica**
**Can't guarantee a seat is sold only once**: an **offline replica** doesn't know about other replicas' **bookings**
**CRDT-style merging** doesn't protect **global invariants**
a.foot: Confirm the purchase through an **authoritative coordination step** before **promising the seat**.

check.q: A retailer composes its commerce stack from a vendor cart, a vendor tax engine, in-house pricing and a headless CMS (MACH). Two years in, nobody knows who owns checkout failures. What went wrong?

a.lead: **Integration became the architecture** without a **capability map** that names **owners** → MACH turned into **distributed procurement**.
items: Each **packaged business capability** needs a **clear owner** and **integration contracts**
**Integration**, **identity** and **cost** across many vendors are **routinely underestimated**

check.q: A 12-developer company plans to build an internal developer platform with golden paths and self-service templates. Is it worth it?

items: **Platform engineering** pays off when **cognitive load** limits delivery **across many teams**
Must be **run as a product**, measured by **adoption** and **DORA metrics**
For **12 developers** → **shared templates** and a **simple pipeline** may be enough
a.foot: **Risk at any size**: the platform team becomes a **gatekeeper** instead of an **enabler**.

exam_angles.q: A bank wants to modernise a 15-year-old monolithic loan system used by 300 branches while continuing to issue loans every day. Propose a target style and a migration approach, and name the two biggest trade-offs.

sub: Route **one capability at a time** to new services
Not a **big-bang rewrite**, which would **stop loan issuance**
**Operational overhead** → invest in **observability** and **platform automation** before the number of services grows

exam_angles.q: Design a data architecture for a ride-hailing company that needs surge pricing within 5 seconds of demand changes and nightly retraining on 3 years of trips. Justify Lambda or Kappa, and say what would change your choice.

items: **Speed layer**: processes the **trip-event stream** → **near-real-time surge prices**
**Batch layer**: holds **full history**, **retrains models nightly**; remains the **accurate source of truth**
**Serving layer**: **merges the results**
**Cost**: **two pipelines** with logic that must **stay consistent**
**What would change it → Kappa**: if reprocessing can be done by **replaying the stream** within the **nightly window**; trades the second pipeline for **harder stateful stream processing**
a.foot: **Event-driven ingestion** keeps **producers decoupled** either way.

exam_angles.q: A government services app must reach all citizens, including those on old phones. It needs form-filling that survives a dropped connection, and a later phase adds reading ID cards over NFC at kiosks. Native or PWA? Give the design implications for the backend services.

a.lead: **Start with a PWA**; add a native kiosk app for the NFC phase.

sub: **Broad reach**, **no install barrier**, **one codebase**, **instant updates** → suit a **citizen service**

items.t: **Native or cross-platform native kiosk app for NFC**

sub: APIs must accept **delayed, batched submissions idempotently** and **handle conflicts**
A **separate backend for each experience (BFF)** may serve **web and kiosk** clients

exam_angles.q: An e-commerce site handles normal traffic but fails on Black Friday at 12 times the load: the database's write capacity is exhausted and checkout slows everything else. Apply the AKF scale cube to the problem and name a side effect of each change.

items.t: **x axis**: **load-balanced clones** of the **stateless web tier**, plus **read replicas**
**y axis**: split **checkout** into its own **service and store** → it **scales and fails independently**
**z axis**: **shard orders** by **customer or region** to **spread writes** → **the fix for exhausted write capacity**

a.foot: Add a **queue** in front of order processing to **level the peak**.

exam_angles.q: A global SaaS needs sub-100 ms response for login and personalisation worldwide, must keep EU data in the EU, and had an outage last year where one bad deploy hit every tenant. Which modern archetypes would you combine, and what are their costs?

sub: Keep **EU tenants' data in EU cells**

items: **Platform with GitOps** → operates **N cells consistently**

sub: **Eventual consistency** and **limited runtimes** at the edge

exam_angles.q: A new product will have 3 developers at launch, sporadic traffic from 0 to 2,000 requests a minute, and a plan to grow to 6 teams in 2 years. Compare monolith, microservices and serverless, and recommend a path.

a.lead: **Recommend a modular monolith**, or a few **functions with a hexagonal core** for the **spiky parts**.
items: **Modular monolith**: minimises **deployment and network complexity** for **3 developers**, but **scales as one unit**
**Microservices**: **independent scaling and releases**, but bring **partial failures**, **data coordination** and **operational overhead** the team **can't afford yet**
**Serverless**: suits the **sporadic load** and **costs little when idle**, but brings **cold starts**, **runtime limits** and **lock-in**
a.foot: Keep **clear module boundaries** so services can be **extracted** as the **6 teams** arrive.
